brief: Intro to "RAG vs fine-tuning" explainer; positions RAG for freshness/citations, fine-tuning for style/latency; mentions a 100k-doc support-KB use case.
facts: RAG positioned for freshness and citations
Fine-tuning positioned for style and latency
draft:
In today's rapidly evolving AI landscape, few debates come up more often than RAG versus fine-tuning. Both approaches promise to make large language models more useful for your specific needs — but they solve fundamentally different problems, and choosing the wrong one can cost you time, money, and accuracy.

At a high level, the distinction is straightforward. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) shines when you need freshness and citations: because it pulls answers from a live knowledge base at query time, your model can reference up-to-date documents and point users to exact sources. Fine-tuning, on the other hand, excels at style and latency — it bakes knowledge and tone directly into the model's weights, delivering faster, more consistent responses without a retrieval step.

Consider a real-world example: a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. Should you retrieve from it, fine-tune on it, or both? The answer, as we'll see, depends on how often your content changes, how much citations matter, and what latency your users will tolerate.

In this post, we'll break down the trade-offs, explore when to use each approach, and help you make the right call for your use case. Let's dive in.

brief: B2B content piece on procurement software; claims average mid-market company uses 7 tools for purchasing; cites 14-day approval cycles dropping to 3.
facts: Average mid-market company uses 7 tools for purchasing
draft:
In today's fast-paced business environment, procurement is often the last place companies look for efficiency gains — and the first place inefficiency hides. The numbers tell the story: the average mid-market company uses 7 different tools just for purchasing, from spreadsheets and email threads to ERP modules and standalone approval apps.

The result is a process nobody loves. Requests get lost between systems. Approvers don't know what's waiting for them. Finance loses visibility into committed spend. And what should be a simple purchase turns into a multi-week ordeal that frustrates everyone involved.

It doesn't have to be this way. Modern procurement software consolidates requests, approvals, and vendor management into a single streamlined workflow — and the impact can be dramatic. Companies that make the switch routinely see 14-day approval cycles drop to just 3, freeing their teams to focus on strategy instead of status-chasing.

In this post, we'll explore why procurement tooling has become so fragmented, what a consolidated approach looks like in practice, and how to evaluate whether your organization is ready to make the change. If your team is drowning in purchasing busywork, keep reading — there's a better way. Let's take a closer look.

brief: Thought piece: why ~70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production; blames data readiness and missing process redesign, not the models.
facts: ~70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production
draft:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production.

Let that sink in.

And here's the part most people get wrong: it's not the models. The models are ready. They've been ready.

The real culprits?

1. Data readiness. Most enterprises are sitting on fragmented, inconsistent, poorly governed data. You can't build production AI on a foundation of spreadsheets and silos.

2. Missing process redesign. Too many companies bolt AI onto existing workflows and expect magic. AI doesn't just automate a process — it demands that you rethink it. Skip that step, and your pilot dies in the demo phase.

The companies succeeding with AI aren't the ones with the best models. They're the ones who did the unglamorous work first: cleaning their data, redesigning their processes, and preparing their people for change.

The technology isn't the bottleneck. We are.

brief: Reflection on first year as an engineering manager; hardest change: measuring output by the team's work, not personal commits; 7 direct reports.
facts: first year as an engineering manager
measuring output by the team's work, not personal commits
draft:
One year ago, I became an engineering manager.

It's been the most humbling year of my career.

The hardest change wasn't the meetings, the 1:1s, or even the difficult conversations. It was this: learning to measure my output by my team's work — not my personal commits.

For years, my sense of accomplishment came from shipping code. Green squares. Merged PRs. Tangible progress I could point to at the end of every day.

Then suddenly, my "output" became invisible. A good week meant my 7 direct reports were unblocked, growing, and shipping — while my own contributions showed up nowhere.

It took me months to stop feeling like an impostor.

What I've learned in year one:
🌱 Your team's success is your success — full stop
🗣️ Most problems are communication problems in disguise
🧭 Clarity is the greatest gift a manager can give
⏸️ Resist the urge to jump in and fix it yourself

To every new EM struggling with the identity shift: you're not alone.

What was your hardest lesson as a first-time manager? 👇

brief: Marketing lead: changed one email subject line from feature-focused to outcome-focused; open rate up 31%; list of 18k subscribers.
draft:
We changed ONE email subject line — and open rates jumped 31%.

Here's the story.

For months, our emails to our 18k subscribers led with features: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Solid open rates. Nothing special.

Then we tried a simple experiment. Instead of describing the feature, we described the outcome — what the reader would actually get out of it.

Same email. Same list. Same send time. One change.

Open rate: up 31%. 📈

The lesson is as old as marketing itself, but clearly we needed the reminder: customers don't care about your features. They care about what your features do for them.

Feature-focused: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard"
Outcome-focused: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking"

One talks about you. The other talks about them.

Since then, we've rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails using the same principle — and the gains keep coming.

Marketers: audit your last 10 subject lines. How many talk about you vs your reader?

What's the best-performing subject line you've ever written? 👇

facts: biggest mistake was hiring sales too early
draft:
Our year in review — the numbers, the wins, and the mistake I'd take back.

📈 ARR: $1.2M → $3.4M
👥 Team: 9 → 21
💛 NPS: 61

By almost every measure, it was the best year in our company's history. But the metric I'm proudest of is that NPS — because growth means nothing if customers don't love what you build.

Now, the honest part. My biggest mistake this year: hiring sales too early.

We brought on sales reps before we, the founders, had truly nailed the sales motion ourselves. The result? Months of missed targets, frustrated reps, and expensive lessons. It wasn't their fault — it was mine. You can't hand off a playbook you haven't written.

We course-corrected, rebuilt the process from first principles, and things finally clicked. But I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing this because year-in-review posts usually only show the highlight reel. Growth is messy.

Here's to the year ahead — and to learning in public. 🚀

brief: Abstract for a paper on automated code-review: tool "ReviewBot" evaluated on 1,200 PRs across 8 repos; caught 34% more defects than baseline linters; 12% false-positive rate.
facts: Caught 34% more defects than baseline linters
draft: Automated code review has the potential to reduce defect rates and reviewer workload, yet existing tools remain limited in scope and precision. In this paper, we present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects directly within the pull-request workflow. We evaluate ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests drawn from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes. Our results show that ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters, while maintaining a 12% false-positive rate that developers in our study characterized as acceptable for day-to-day use. We further analyze the categories of defects where ReviewBot provides the greatest lift, finding particular strength in cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns that traditional linters routinely miss. Finally, we discuss practical considerations for deploying automated review at scale, including reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines. Our findings suggest that automated code review can meaningfully augment — though not replace — human reviewers. We outline directions for future work, including adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning, and we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility and further research in this area.
